rule-low-autonomy.detail: Loads that can't wait for sun — fridge/freezer, a pump, medical gear, always-on connectivity — can take the bank to empty before noon in a single overcast stretch.
rule-low-autonomy.fix: Plan 2-3 days of autonomy for critical setups and re-check the battery size.
rule-low-autonomy.title: One day of battery autonomy is thin for critical loads

rule-surge-headroom.detail: The worst startup spike exceeds roughly twice the continuous inverter your running watts call for — past the ~2x surge ceiling a right-sized inverter typically tolerates.
rule-surge-headroom.fix: Step up to a larger continuous inverter (so its surge clears the spike), or add a soft starter to that appliance.
rule-surge-headroom.title: A motor load can stall a right-sized inverter on startup

note-air-compressor.detail: A 1,500W compressor can spike past 3,000W when the motor unloads and restarts. Pancake and twin-stack units routinely stall small inverters mid-task.
note-air-compressor.fix: Run shop tools on a 3,000W+ low-frequency inverter, or add a soft-start / larger run capacitor. Don't size to the running watts.
note-air-compressor.title: Air compressors have brutal startup inrush

note-cpap.detail: Running a CPAP through an AC inverter wastes power on overhead, and the heated humidifier roughly doubles the draw. A single cloudy night can't be allowed to cut therapy.
note-cpap.fix: Power it from 12V DC where possible, turn off the heated humidifier to cut draw ~50%, and size 2+ days of autonomy.
note-cpap.title: CPAP is life-support-adjacent — plan it conservatively

note-electric-cooking.detail: A 2,000–2,500W resistive element running through a meal is a huge, sustained draw — the kind of load that doubles a modest system's size for one appliance.
note-electric-cooking.fix: Cook on propane off-grid. Reserve electric cooking for an Instant Pot / induction burner used briefly, and size for those instead.
note-electric-cooking.title: Electric ovens and ranges are rarely solar-viable

note-ev-charger.detail: 1,400W for 8 hours is ~11 kWh a day — frequently more than everything else on the system put together. It will quietly drain the bank overnight.
note-ev-charger.fix: Charge the vehicle from grid or a generator, not the off-grid battery. If solar-charging, dedicate a separate array sized just for it.
note-ev-charger.title: Even Level 1 EV charging can outweigh your whole house

note-fridge-freezer.detail: Compressors pull 3–5× their running watts to start, and because they cycle 24/7 they quietly dominate your daily watt-hours — especially in summer heat. Modified-sine power makes them buzz and shortens compressor life.
note-fridge-freezer.fix: Pure-sine inverter, and size the battery for the all-day cycling load. In hot climates add ~30% to the fridge's estimated draw.
note-fridge-freezer.title: Fridges and freezers surge hard and never turn off

note-hair-dryer.detail: 1,500W plus a motor surge is a lot for a small portable system, even though it only runs a few minutes.
note-hair-dryer.fix: Use the low/warm setting (~750W) or run it on a 2,000W+ inverter. It's the surge, not the daily energy, that matters here.
note-hair-dryer.title: Hair dryers are brief but trip undersized inverters

note-microwave.detail: The wattage on the door is cooking output, not input draw. The real load on your inverter is 40–70% higher, and it hits instantly.
note-microwave.fix: Size the inverter to the input draw (2,000W+ pure sine), and keep run times short — microwaves are fine off-grid in bursts, not for long cooks.
note-microwave.title: A "1,000W" microwave actually pulls ~1,500–1,700W from the battery

note-oxygen-concentrator.detail: ~300W continuous (with a 600W startup surge) for 12–24 hours a day is one of the heaviest sustained draws a home system will see, and it can't fail.
note-oxygen-concentrator.fix: Build a robust battery bank with 2–3 days autonomy and keep a generator as medical backup. Don't run it on a portable power station rated for occasional use.
note-oxygen-concentrator.title: An oxygen concentrator is a serious continuous medical load

note-resistive-heat.detail: A 1,500W heater run a few hours a day can need more panel and battery than the rest of your loads combined. Solar almost never pencils out for primary electric heat.
note-resistive-heat.fix: Heat with propane or wood and keep the electric heater as occasional spot backup only. If you must, budget a much larger array + bank specifically for it.
note-resistive-heat.title: Electric resistance heat is the #1 way off-grid systems get blown out

note-starlink.detail: At ~75–100W running 24/7, that's ~1.8–2.4 kWh every day — and in low-sun winter it's frequently the load that drains the battery first.
note-starlink.fix: Size the battery for 2–3 cloudy days, or put Starlink on a scheduled/idle power cut overnight. It's a continuous load, not a peak one.
note-starlink.title: Always-on Starlink is often the single biggest line item

note-sump-pump.detail: Motor inrush roughly doubles the running watts, and the times you need it most (storms) are exactly when there's no sun to recharge.
note-sump-pump.fix: Give it real inverter surge headroom and 2–3 days of battery autonomy so a multi-day storm doesn't outlast the bank.
note-sump-pump.title: A sump pump is critical and surges — don't run it on the edge

note-tankless-water-heater.detail: Whole-house electric tankless units draw 7,000–18,000W. Even the point-of-use 3,500W version strains most off-grid inverters and batteries.
note-tankless-water-heater.fix: Use propane on-demand or a solar-thermal / batch heater. Don't try to size a battery bank around instant electric hot water.
note-tankless-water-heater.title: Electric tankless water heaters are not an off-grid load

note-well-pump.detail: A ½ HP pump runs at ~750W but its motor draws 3–5× that for a split second on every start (locked-rotor inrush) — a 2,000–3,500W spike. Plenty of 2,000W inverters shut down on it even though the running number looks fine.
note-well-pump.fix: Use a low-frequency (transformer-based) inverter rated 3,000W+, or fit the pump with a soft starter / CSCR control box. Pure sine only.
note-well-pump.title: A submersible well pump can trip an inverter that's sized for its running watts

note-window-ac.detail: A 500W window unit spikes near 1,500W the instant the compressor kicks in, and it does that every cycle. On a modified-sine inverter the compressor buzzes, runs hot, and fails early.
note-window-ac.fix: Run AC only on a pure-sine inverter with real surge headroom, or add a soft-start kit. Plan battery for the cycling draw, not the nameplate watts.
note-window-ac.title: Air conditioner compressors surge ~3× on startup

ok-clean.detail: Nothing here trips the usual off-grid traps — no brutal motor surges, runaway resistive heat, or critical loads left without buffer.
ok-clean.title: No red flags for this load list
